note.explanation: Chemical bonding explains how atoms or ions are held together. The main types are ionic, covalent, coordinate covalent and metallic bonding. Bonding and the forces between particles help explain the properties of substances.
examples: In NaCl, sodium ions and chloride ions are held together by ionic attraction.
In a metal, positive metal ions are held together by attraction to free-moving electrons.
note.checkAnswer: An ionic bond is the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
note.simple: Atoms join or pack together in different ways. The way they are joined helps decide whether a substance is hard, conducts electricity, or melts easily.
note.checkQuestion: What holds the positive metal ions together in a metallic bond?
note.title: Chemical Bonding: Bonds and Properties
steps: Identify the particles in the substance: atoms, ions, or metal ions and electrons.
Identify the bond or attraction holding those particles together.
Use the bond and particle arrangement to explain the property being asked about.
note.answer: A chemical bond is an attractive force that holds atoms or ions together.

mcqs.stem: Q3.1. When molten copper and molten Zinc are mixed together, they give rise to a new substance called brass. Predict what type of bond is formed between copper and zinc.
rationales: A coordinate covalent bond is not the bonding between the metal atoms in brass.
An ionic bond involves oppositely charged ions, not the metal atoms in brass.
A metallic bond holds metal atoms together, as in brass.
A covalent bond involves sharing electron pairs between non-metal atoms.

mcqs.stem: Q3.2. Which element is capable of forming all the three types of bonds; covalent, coordinate covalent and ionic?
rationales: Carbon commonly forms covalent bonds but is not the element identified as forming all three types here.
Oxygen forms covalent bonds, coordinate covalent bonds, and ionic compounds with metals.
Magnesium mainly forms ionic and metallic bonds, not all three types listed.
Silicon commonly forms covalent bonds, but it is not the expected answer for all three types.

options: Because in water, the atomic size of oxygen is smaller than that of sulphur
Because water is a polar compound and there exists strong forces of attraction between its molecules
Because H₂O molecule is lighter than H₂S
Because water can easily freeze into ice
mcqs.stem: Q3.3. Why is H₂O a liquid while H₂S is a gas?
rationales: The size difference does not by itself explain why water is liquid at ordinary conditions.
Water molecules form strong intermolecular attractions, including hydrogen bonds, so water is liquid while H₂S is a gas.
H₂O is not lighter than H₂S, so this option is incorrect.
The ability of water to freeze does not explain why it is liquid while H₂S is a gas.

mcqs.stem: Q3.4. Which of the following bonds is expected to be the weakest?
rationales: The C–C bond is not the weakest bond in this list.
The Cl–Cl bond is stronger than the F–F bond.
The O–O bond is not the weakest bond in this list.
The F–F bond is weakest because the small fluorine atoms have strong repulsion between their lone pairs.

mcqs.stem: Q3.5. Which form of carbon is used as a lubricant?
rationales: Coal is not the form of carbon commonly used as a lubricant.
Diamond has a rigid three-dimensional structure and is not used as a lubricant.
Graphite has layers that can slide over one another, so it is used as a lubricant.
Charcoal is not the form of carbon commonly used as a lubricant.

mcqs.stem: Q3.6. Keeping in view the intermolecular forces of attraction, indicate which compound has the highest boiling point.
rationales: Water molecules form especially strong hydrogen bonds, giving H₂O the highest boiling point in this list.
H₂S does not have hydrogen bonding as strong as that in water.
HF has hydrogen bonding, but its boiling point is lower than that of water.
NH₃ has hydrogen bonding, but its boiling point is lower than that of water.

mcqs.stem: Q3.7. Which metal has the lowest melting point?
rationales: Lithium has a higher melting point than rubidium.
Sodium has a higher melting point than rubidium.
Potassium has a higher melting point than rubidium.
Rubidium has the lowest melting point among the listed metals.

mcqs.stem: Q3.8. Which ionic compound has the highest melting point?
rationales: NaCl has the highest melting point among these choices.
KCl has a lower melting point than NaCl.
LiCl has a lower melting point than NaCl.
RbCl has a lower melting point than NaCl.

mcqs.stem: Q3.9. Which compound contains both covalent and ionic bonds?
rationales: MgCl₂ is an ionic compound and does not contain a covalently bonded polyatomic ion.
NH₄Cl has covalent bonds within the ammonium ion and ionic attraction between NH₄⁺ and Cl⁻.
CaO is an ionic compound.
PCl₃ contains covalent bonds but not ionic bonding between ions.

mcqs.stem: Q3.10. Which among the following has a double covalent bond?
rationales: Ethane has a carbon–carbon single bond.
Methane has only single covalent bonds.
Ethylene has a carbon–carbon double bond.
Acetylene has a carbon–carbon triple bond.

written.text: What type of elements lose their outer electron easily and what type of elements gain electron easily?
written.finalAnswer: Metals lose outer electrons easily; non-metals gain electrons easily.

rubric.why: The answer must identify the elements that lose electrons.
rubric.how: State that metals lose their outer electron(s).

rubric.why: The answer must identify the elements that gain electrons.
rubric.how: State that non-metals gain electron(s).

modelAnswer: Metals lose their outer electrons easily.
Non-metals gain electrons easily.

written.text: Why do lower molecular mass covalent compounds exist as gases or low boiling liquids.
written.finalAnswer: They have weak intermolecular forces of attraction, so little energy is needed to separate their molecules.

rubric.why: The explanation must identify the weak attractions between molecules.
rubric.description: States that intermolecular forces are weak.
rubric.how: Name the weak forces between covalent molecules.

rubric.why: The weak attractions explain the low boiling points or gaseous state.
rubric.description: Links weak forces to low boiling points or gases.
rubric.how: Explain that little energy is needed to separate the molecules.

modelAnswer: Lower molecular mass covalent compounds have weak forces of attraction between their molecules.
Little energy is needed to separate their molecules, so they exist as gases or low boiling liquids.

written.text: Give one example of an element which exists as a crystalline solid and it has covalent bonds between its atoms.
written.finalAnswer: Carbon (diamond or graphite).

rubric.why: The answer must name an appropriate element.
rubric.how: Write carbon as the element.

rubric.why: An appropriate crystalline form is needed to complete the example.
rubric.description: Names a crystalline form of carbon.
rubric.how: Give diamond or graphite as the form.

modelAnswer: Carbon exists as a crystalline solid in forms such as diamond.
Its atoms are joined by covalent bonds.

written.text: Which property of metals makes them malleable and ductile?
written.finalAnswer: The non-directional nature of the metallic bond makes metals malleable and ductile.

rubric.why: The answer must relate the property to metallic bonding.
rubric.how: Name the metallic bond as the relevant feature.

rubric.why: The non-directional bonding allows layers of metal ions to move without breaking the bonding.
rubric.description: Explains why the metal can be shaped.
rubric.how: State that layers can slide while the metallic attraction remains.

modelAnswer: The non-directional nature of the metallic bond allows layers of metal ions to slide over one another.
Therefore, metals are malleable and ductile.

written.text: Is coordinate covalent bond a strong bond?
written.finalAnswer: Yes. A coordinate covalent bond is a strong covalent bond once formed.

rubric.why: The response must clearly answer the yes-or-no question.
rubric.how: Answer yes.

rubric.why: The answer should identify the strength of the bond after formation.
rubric.description: States that it is strong once formed.
rubric.how: Explain that it is strong like an ordinary covalent bond.

modelAnswer: Yes, a coordinate covalent bond is a strong bond.
Once formed, it behaves like an ordinary covalent bond.

written.text: Write down dot and cross formula of HNO₃.
written.finalAnswer: H–O–N(=O)→O (one accepted dot-and-cross arrangement, showing a coordinate bond).

rubric.why: The answer must show the correct atoms connected in nitric acid.
rubric.description: Shows the atom connectivity of HNO₃.
rubric.how: Draw or write the H–O–N and N–O connections, including an N=O bond.

rubric.why: The dot-and-cross formula must identify the coordinate bond and its electron-pair donation.
rubric.how: Mark the coordinate bond with an arrow or show that the donated pair comes from a lone pair.

modelAnswer: A dot-and-cross formula shows the arrangement H–O–N(=O)→O.
The arrow represents a coordinate covalent bond, with the shared pair donated by one atom.

written.text: Why HF is a liquid while HCl is a gas?
written.finalAnswer: HF molecules form strong hydrogen bonds; HCl molecules have weaker intermolecular forces, so HF is liquid while HCl is gas.

rubric.why: The key reason HF has a higher boiling point is its strong intermolecular attraction.
rubric.description: Explains the strong attraction between HF molecules.
rubric.how: State that HF molecules form strong hydrogen bonds.

rubric.why: A comparison with HCl is needed to explain the different physical states.
rubric.how: State that HCl has weaker intermolecular forces.

rubric.why: The explanation must connect the forces to the stated physical states.
rubric.description: Gives the correct states and links them to the attraction.
rubric.how: Conclude that HF is liquid and HCl is gas at ordinary conditions.

modelAnswer: HF molecules form strong hydrogen bonds with one another.
HCl molecules do not form hydrogen bonds and have weaker intermolecular forces.
More energy is needed to separate HF molecules than HCl molecules.
Therefore, HF is a liquid while HCl is a gas at ordinary conditions.

written.text: Why covalent compounds are generally not soluble in water?
written.finalAnswer: Most covalent compounds are non-polar, whereas water is polar, so they do not dissolve in water.

rubric.why: The answer should describe the general polarity of covalent compounds.
rubric.description: Identifies covalent compounds as generally non-polar.
rubric.how: State that they are generally non-polar.

rubric.why: The polarity of water is needed for the comparison.
rubric.how: State that water is a polar solvent.

rubric.why: The polarity difference explains the general lack of solubility.
rubric.description: Connects the polarity difference to insolubility.
rubric.how: Conclude that most non-polar covalent compounds do not dissolve in polar water.

modelAnswer: Most covalent compounds are non-polar.
Water is a polar solvent.
A non-polar substance generally does not dissolve in a polar solvent.
Therefore, covalent compounds are generally not soluble in water.

written.text: How do metals conduct heat?
written.finalAnswer: Free electrons transfer kinetic energy through the metal and conduct heat.

rubric.why: Free electrons are the main carriers of heat energy in metals.
rubric.description: Identifies the mobile electrons in a metal.
rubric.how: State that metals contain free or mobile electrons.

rubric.why: The answer must explain what the electrons carry through the metal.
rubric.description: Describes energy transfer by the electrons.
rubric.how: Say that the electrons gain and transfer energy.

rubric.why: This links electron movement to the observed property.
rubric.description: Concludes that heat is conducted through the metal.
rubric.how: State that the transfer makes metals conduct heat.

modelAnswer: Metals contain free-moving electrons.
These electrons gain kinetic energy from the hot part of the metal.
They move through the metal and transfer energy to other particles.
Thus, metals conduct heat.

written.text: How many oxides does nitrogen form. Write down the formulae of oxides?
written.finalAnswer: Five: N₂O, NO, N₂O₃, NO₂ and N₂O₅.

rubric.why: The number of oxides requested must be stated.
rubric.description: States the number of nitrogen oxides.
rubric.how: Write that nitrogen forms five oxides.

rubric.why: The first oxide must be correctly named by formula.
rubric.how: Write N₂O.

rubric.why: The middle oxide formulae are part of the requested list.
rubric.how: Write both formulae correctly.

rubric.why: The remaining oxide formulae complete the list.
rubric.how: Write both formulae correctly.

modelAnswer: Nitrogen forms five oxides.
Their formulae are N₂O, NO, N₂O₃, NO₂ and N₂O₅.

written.text: What will happen if NaBr is treated with AgNO₃ in water?
written.finalAnswer: A yellow precipitate of AgBr forms, and NaNO₃ remains in solution.

rubric.why: Silver bromide is the insoluble product formed in the reaction.
rubric.how: Name or write AgBr.

rubric.why: The observation is evidence that a reaction has occurred.
rubric.how: State that a pale yellow precipitate forms.

rubric.why: The other product should also be identified.
rubric.how: Write NaNO₃ as the other product.

rubric.why: A balanced equation shows the reaction products correctly.
rubric.how: Write NaBr + AgNO₃ → AgBr + NaNO₃.

modelAnswer: NaBr(aq) + AgNO₃(aq) → AgBr(s) + NaNO₃(aq)
A pale yellow precipitate of AgBr forms.

written.text: Why does iodine exist as a solid while Cl₂ exist as a gas?
written.finalAnswer: I₂ molecules are larger and have stronger intermolecular forces than Cl₂ molecules, so iodine is solid while chlorine is a gas.

rubric.why: The larger iodine molecules have more electrons and stronger dispersion forces.
rubric.how: State that I₂ molecules are larger than Cl₂ molecules.

rubric.why: The difference in intermolecular force strength explains the difference in state.
rubric.description: Explains the stronger attraction between iodine molecules.
rubric.how: Link larger molecules with stronger intermolecular attractions.

rubric.why: The conclusion must correctly give the physical states.
rubric.how: Conclude that iodine is solid and chlorine is gas at ordinary conditions.

modelAnswer: I₂ molecules are larger than Cl₂ molecules.
The larger I₂ molecules have stronger intermolecular forces of attraction.
More energy is needed to separate iodine molecules.
Therefore, iodine is a solid while Cl₂ is a gas at ordinary conditions.

written.text: Explain the formation of an ionic bond and a covalent bond.
written.finalAnswer: An ionic bond forms by electron transfer and attraction between oppositely charged ions; a covalent bond forms when atoms share electron pair(s).

rubric.why: Electron transfer is the key step in ionic bond formation.
rubric.how: State that one atom transfers electron(s) to another.

rubric.why: The resulting ions create the attraction that holds the ionic compound together.
rubric.how: State that positive and negative ions form.

rubric.why: The attraction between the ions is the ionic bond.
rubric.description: Defines the ionic bond as an attraction.
rubric.how: Name the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

rubric.why: Sharing electron pairs is the key feature of covalent bonding.
rubric.how: State that atoms share electron pair(s).

rubric.why: The answer must connect sharing to covalent bond formation.
rubric.description: Identifies the shared pair as the covalent bond.
rubric.how: Conclude that the shared electron pair(s) form a covalent bond.

modelAnswer: In ionic bond formation, one atom transfers electron(s) to another atom.
The atoms become oppositely charged ions.
The electrostatic attraction between these ions forms an ionic bond.
In covalent bond formation, atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
The shared electron pair(s) form a covalent bond.

written.text: How do ions arrange themselve to form NaCl crystal.
written.finalAnswer: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions form a regular three-dimensional lattice, with each ion surrounded by six ions of the opposite charge.

rubric.why: The crystal's regular three-dimensional arrangement is essential to its structure.
rubric.how: State that the ions form a regular three-dimensional lattice.

rubric.why: Both kinds of ions in sodium chloride must be identified.
rubric.how: Include Na⁺ ions.

rubric.why: Both kinds of ions in sodium chloride must be identified.
rubric.how: Include Cl⁻ ions.

rubric.why: The alternating nearest-neighbour arrangement explains the crystal packing.
rubric.how: State that each ion is surrounded by six oppositely charged ions.

modelAnswer: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions arrange themselves alternately in a regular three-dimensional lattice.
Each Na⁺ ion is surrounded by six Cl⁻ ions.
Each Cl⁻ ion is surrounded by six Na⁺ ions.
The electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions holds the crystal together.

written.text: Explain the properties of metals keeping in view the nature of metallic bond.
written.finalAnswer: Metallic bonding gives metals conductivity, malleability, ductility and generally high melting points because of free electrons and non-directional attraction between metal ions and electrons.

rubric.why: The metallic-bond model must be described.
rubric.description: Describes metal ions surrounded by electrons.
rubric.how: Mention positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.

rubric.why: Mobile electrons explain electrical and thermal conductivity.
rubric.how: Explain that free electrons carry charge and heat.

rubric.why: Non-directional bonding explains why metals can be shaped.
rubric.how: State that layers can slide while attraction remains.

rubric.why: Strong attraction helps explain metals' generally high melting points and strength.
rubric.description: Describes the strength of the metallic attraction.
rubric.how: State that attraction between ions and electrons is strong.

rubric.why: The explanation should connect the bonding model to metal properties.
rubric.how: Name a relevant property, such as malleability, ductility or a generally high melting point.

modelAnswer: A metal consists of positive metal ions surrounded by a sea of delocalised electrons.
The free electrons move through the metal and conduct electricity and heat.
The metallic bond is non-directional, so layers of ions can slide over one another while attraction is maintained.
Therefore, metals are malleable and ductile.
The strong attraction between positive ions and electrons also helps give metals high melting points.

written.text: Compare the properties of ionic and covalent compounds.
written.finalAnswer: Ionic compounds are usually hard crystalline solids with high melting points, conduct electricity when molten or in solution, and are often water-soluble; covalent compounds usually have lower melting and boiling points, do not conduct electricity, and are generally not soluble in water.

rubric.why: The comparison should include a characteristic physical property of ionic compounds.
rubric.how: State that ionic compounds are crystalline solids and/or have high melting points.

rubric.why: Ionic conductivity depends on mobile ions.
rubric.description: Explains when ionic compounds conduct electricity.
rubric.how: State that they conduct when molten or dissolved because their ions can move.

rubric.why: Molecular covalent compounds commonly have lower melting and boiling points.
rubric.how: State that they generally have low melting or boiling points.

rubric.why: The comparison should include electrical conductivity.
rubric.description: States that covalent compounds generally do not conduct electricity.
rubric.how: State that they usually do not conduct electricity.

rubric.why: Solubility is another standard comparison between the two types.
rubric.how: State the general solubility pattern for ionic and covalent compounds.

modelAnswer: Ionic compounds are usually hard crystalline solids with high melting and boiling points because of strong attraction between oppositely charged ions.
They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water because their ions can move.
Many ionic compounds are soluble in water.
Covalent compounds usually have low melting and boiling points because the forces between their molecules are weak.
They generally do not conduct electricity and are usually not soluble in water.

written.text: How will you explain the electrical conductivity of graphite crystals?
written.finalAnswer: Each carbon atom in graphite shares electrons with three other carbon atoms; the remaining electrons are delocalised and move through the layers, conducting electricity.

rubric.why: The bonding arrangement leaves one electron from each carbon atom available for delocalisation.
rubric.how: State that each carbon bonds to three neighbouring carbon atoms.

rubric.why: The mobile electrons carry charge through graphite.
rubric.how: State that the remaining electrons are delocalised.

rubric.why: Movement of delocalised electrons explains conductivity.
rubric.description: Links electron movement to electrical conduction.
rubric.how: Explain that the electrons move through the layers and carry charge.

modelAnswer: Each carbon atom in graphite is covalently bonded to three other carbon atoms.
One electron from each carbon atom is not used in these bonds.
These electrons are delocalised and can move through the layers.
The moving electrons carry charge.
Therefore, graphite crystals conduct electricity.

written.text: Why are metals usually hard and heavy?
written.finalAnswer: Strong metallic attraction holds closely packed metal atoms together, and their high density makes them heavy.

rubric.why: Strong bonding helps account for the hardness of metals.
rubric.description: Explains metal hardness using metallic bonding.
rubric.how: State that strong metallic attraction holds the particles together.

rubric.why: Close packing contributes to the compact structure of metals.
rubric.description: Describes the close arrangement of metal particles.
rubric.how: State that the metal atoms or ions are closely packed.

rubric.why: Density explains why metals are heavy for their size.
rubric.how: Mention the high density of metals.

rubric.why: The response must address both properties in the question.
rubric.how: Conclude that metals are usually hard and heavy.

modelAnswer: Strong metallic attraction holds the metal particles together firmly, making metals usually hard.
Metal particles are closely packed in a lattice.
This close packing gives metals a high density.
Therefore, metals are usually hard and heavy.

written.text: The formula of AlCl₃ in vapour phase is Al₂Cl₆ which means it exists as a dimer. Explain the bonding between its two molecules?
written.finalAnswer: Two AlCl₃ molecules form Al₂Cl₆ when lone pairs from bridging chlorine atoms are donated to electron-deficient aluminium atoms, forming coordinate covalent bonds.

rubric.why: Electron-deficient aluminium explains why the dimer forms.
rubric.description: Explains the electron deficiency of AlCl₃.
rubric.how: State that aluminium in AlCl₃ has an incomplete octet.

rubric.why: A chlorine lone pair supplies the electron pair for the coordinate bond.
rubric.how: State that a chlorine atom donates a lone pair.

rubric.why: The bond between the units must be identified as coordinate covalent.
rubric.description: Names the bond formed between the molecules.
rubric.how: Explain that the donated pair forms a coordinate covalent bond to an Al atom of the other molecule.

rubric.why: The explanation should connect the bonding to the dimer formula.
rubric.description: States that the joined units form the dimer.
rubric.how: Conclude that two AlCl₃ molecules form Al₂Cl₆.

modelAnswer: In AlCl₃, the aluminium atom is electron-deficient and has an incomplete octet.
A chlorine atom of one AlCl₃ molecule donates a lone pair to the aluminium atom of another molecule.
This forms a coordinate covalent bond between the two molecules.
The two chlorine atoms act as bridges between the aluminium atoms.
Thus, two AlCl₃ molecules form the dimer Al₂Cl₆.

written.text: Explain the structure of sand (SiO₂).
written.finalAnswer: Sand has a giant three-dimensional covalent network; each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms, and each oxygen atom is shared between two silicon atoms.

rubric.why: The extended network, rather than separate molecules, describes the structure of silica.
rubric.how: State that SiO₂ forms a giant three-dimensional covalent network.

rubric.why: The silicon coordination is a key part of the network structure.
rubric.description: Gives the number of oxygen atoms bonded to silicon.
rubric.how: State that each silicon atom bonds to four oxygen atoms.

rubric.why: Oxygen sharing connects the silica network throughout the structure.
rubric.how: State that each oxygen atom is shared by two silicon atoms.

rubric.why: Covalent bonds hold the structure together.
rubric.description: Identifies the bonds in the network.
rubric.how: State that strong covalent bonds join the atoms.

modelAnswer: Sand (SiO₂) has a giant three-dimensional covalent structure.
Each silicon atom is covalently bonded to four oxygen atoms.
Each oxygen atom is shared between two silicon atoms.
Strong covalent bonds extend throughout the structure.

examTips: Section A tests quick recognition of bond types, structures and properties; learn how each property follows from bonding.
Short questions often ask for a definition, example, or one reason. Give the key term directly and add the reason if asked why.
Constructed-response questions commonly ask you to explain a state, reaction, or property. State the relevant force or particle movement, then link it to the result.
For descriptive answers, compare both substances using paired points, such as melting point, conductivity and solubility.
For bonding diagrams or formulae, show the particles and bonding clearly; label coordinate bonds and electron transfer or sharing where relevant.
For reactions, write the correct products and balance the equation; also state an observation such as a precipitate when requested.

hints: Think about whether NaBr and AgNO₃ contain ions that can exchange partners.
Identify the insoluble product AgBr, then write the balanced equation and observation.

solution: AgBr is insoluble and forms a pale yellow precipitate.
yourTurn.answer: A pale yellow precipitate of AgBr forms; NaNO₃ remains in solution.

hints: Compare the size of I₂ and Cl₂ molecules.

solution: I₂ molecules are larger than Cl₂ molecules.

yourTurn.answer: I₂ molecules have stronger intermolecular forces than Cl₂ molecules, so iodine is solid while chlorine is a gas.

steps.why: The electron moves from the sodium atom to the chlorine atom, producing oppositely charged ions.
steps.text: A sodium atom transfers one electron to a chlorine atom.

steps.why: The transfer gives each ion a stable outer electron arrangement.
steps.text: Sodium becomes Na⁺ and chlorine becomes Cl⁻.

steps.why: The opposite charges attract each other.
steps.text: The electrostatic attraction between Na⁺ and Cl⁻ forms an ionic bond.

steps.why: The formula shows the simplest ratio of ions needed to make a neutral compound.
steps.text: The ions combine in a 1:1 ratio to form NaCl.

example.question: Explain the formation of an ionic bond and a covalent bond.
example.answer: An ionic bond forms by electron transfer and attraction between oppositely charged ions. A covalent bond forms when atoms share electron pair(s).

explain.title: Four kinds of bonding
explain.body: Ionic bonding involves electron transfer and attraction between oppositely charged ions. Covalent bonding involves shared electron pairs. In a coordinate covalent bond, one atom supplies both electrons in the shared pair. Metallic bonding is the attraction between positive metal ions and delocalised electrons.

explain.title: Intermolecular forces affect boiling points
explain.body: Small covalent molecules are often gases or low-boiling liquids because the forces between their molecules are weak. Stronger intermolecular attractions need more energy to overcome. Hydrogen bonding helps explain the high boiling points of water and HF.

explain.title: Ionic and covalent substances have different properties
explain.body: Ionic solids have ions arranged in a lattice and usually have high melting points. They conduct electricity when their ions can move, such as when molten or dissolved. Simple covalent molecules generally do not conduct electricity and often have low melting and boiling points.

explain.title: Metals and graphite conduct electricity
explain.body: Metals conduct because their delocalised electrons can move through the structure. In graphite, each carbon atom bonds to three others, leaving electrons free to move along the layers and carry charge.

explain.title: Structures can be simple molecules or giant networks
explain.body: NaCl forms a regular ionic lattice, while silica (SiO₂) forms a giant covalent network. Graphite is made of layers of covalently bonded carbon atoms. These large-scale arrangements help explain hardness, conductivity and melting behaviour.

mistakes: Do not confuse the bonds within a molecule with forces between molecules; boiling a simple molecular substance usually separates molecules, not atoms within them.
Do not say that an ionic solid conducts electricity while its ions are fixed in place; mobile ions are needed for conduction.
Do not say covalent compounds are always insoluble or that every ionic compound is soluble; use the general trend asked for in the question.
When explaining metallic properties, mention the role of mobile electrons and the non-directional metallic bond, not just that metals are strong.
For a precipitate reaction, identify the insoluble product and state the observation clearly.
In a comparison, discuss both substances and use the same property for each side.
